Dolly Parton had a power no president does: the ability to influence basically
anyone for the better.

"I am not political," she once famously said. "I'm more about the person and
about the message."

Compare that to the brute force logic of our politics, where the prevailing
strategy is to win the White House, run up the score in Congress, and bulldoze
the opposition.

Parton showed another way.

In a world of team red and team blue, Dolly was _platinum_. She understood
that the most valuable substance is consensus; and like platinum, it's
precious because it's rare. It can't be forced and must be gathered with
patience and care. Dolly managed this by walking a tightrope.

An early defender of gay marriage, she made her case not by shaming opponents
but with playful self-deprecation, quipping: "Why shouldn't they get to be as
miserable as the rest of us?"

She was a philanthropist but didn't virtue signal, instead preferring to
remain anonymous. For decades, Parton anonymously covered the cost of school
band uniforms at high schools across Tennessee, never publicizing the gesture
or attaching her name to it. (It only came to light when observant fans on
social media noticed a pattern of unexplained donations and connected the dots
back to her.)

Her philanthropy was practical and without ceremony. In her native Appalachian
Tennessee, she launched the "Buddy Program," giving 7th and 8th graders $500
cash from her own pocket if they graduated--slashing the local dropout rate
from 35% to 6%.

The daughter of a poor Tennessee sharecropper, she never forgot where she came
from while never condescending to it either. She founded the Imagination
Library in tribute to her father, whom she called "the smartest man I have
ever known," but who never had the opportunity to learn to read and write. The
program has since mailed more than 300 million free books to children.

Parton's ease across worlds seemed to rest on a genuine respect for other
people's humanity, including those whose lives and work were far removed from
her own. After her death, Eminem revealed that she had privately written to
him following their 2022 induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Though
she acknowledged that she did not know much about rap, Parton told him: "No
matter how complex your world may be, just know you are very special and touch
people in ways you don't even know."

The most frustrating thing about journalism, to me, is when a story only lands
with the side the facts happen to flatter. Dolly could reach all kinds of
people. Now that she's gone, I can't think of anyone who still does. I
certainly don't, and it isn't for lack of trying.

"If you don't like the road you're walking, start paving another one," Dolly
once said.

I'm going to keep trying.
